sources.text: Jesus said to him, “‘You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind.’ This is the first and great commandment. A second likewise is this, ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’

answer: Jesus answered with two commandments. The first and great commandment is “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind” [S1]. He added that a second is like it: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” [S1].

variants.answer: Loving God with all your heart, soul and mind—and, second, loving your neighbor as yourself [S1].

memories: The user likes study notes with headings and bullet points.
variants.answer:
Passage:
- Matthew 22:37-39 [S1]

Key points:
- The first and great commandment: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind” [S1].
- The second is like it: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” [S1].

Reflection:
- Jesus pairs love for God with love for neighbor rather than giving a single rule.

sources.text: In nothing be anxious, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus.

answer: Instead of being anxious, bring every request to God in prayer with thanksgiving, and his peace, which surpasses understanding, will guard your hearts and thoughts in Christ Jesus [S1].

sources.text: “He arose and came to his father. But while he was still far off, his father saw him and was moved with compassion, and ran, fell on his neck, and kissed him.

Luke 15 contains three parables about lost things: a sheep, a coin and a son. They are told in response to Pharisees and scribes who complained that Jesus welcomed sinners and ate with them (Luke 15:1-2).

inputs.question: Give me study notes on the father’s welcome in the parable of the lost son.

answer:
Passage:
- Luke 15:20 [S1]

What the text says:
- The son “arose and came to his father” [S1].
- “while he was still far off,” the father saw him, “was moved with compassion, and ran, fell on his neck, and kissed him” [S1].

Context (commentary):
- Luke 15 has three parables about lost things: a sheep, a coin and a son [S2].
- They answer Pharisees and scribes who complained that Jesus welcomed sinners and ate with them [S2].

For reflection:
- The father acts before the son can speak; how does that shape the picture of welcome?

sources.text: For the wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.
for all have sinned, and fall short of the glory of God;

answer: Romans 6:23 contrasts two outcomes: “the wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord” [S1]. Death is what sin earns; eternal life is a gift. Earlier Paul says “all have sinned, and fall short of the glory of God” [S2], so everyone needs that gift.

memories: The user is new to the Bible and prefers simple explanations.
variants.answer: In simple terms: sin leads to death, but God offers eternal life as a free gift through Jesus [S1]. Paul also says that everyone has sinned [S2], so this gift is for all of us, not something we earn.

sources.text: Now faith is assurance of things hoped for, proof of things not seen.

inputs.question: What does Hebrews 11:1 say about faith?

answer: Hebrews 11:1 defines faith this way: “Now faith is assurance of things hoped for, proof of things not seen” [S1]. Faith is described as confidence about what is hoped for and conviction about what cannot yet be seen [S1].

memories: The user prefers answers as bullet points.
variants.answer:
- Faith is “assurance of things hoped for” [S1].
- Faith is “proof of things not seen” [S1].
- Together: confidence about what is hoped for and conviction about what cannot yet be seen.

sources.text: For I delivered to you first of all that which I also received: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures,

Many scholars regard 1 Corinthians 15:3-5 as an early summary of Christian teaching that Paul had received and passed on, because he introduces it with the language of receiving and delivering tradition.

answer:
In 1 Corinthians 15:3-4 Paul summarises the message he first passed on to the Corinthians: “For I delivered to you first of all that which I also received: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures” [S1].

The passage makes three linked claims. First, Christ died “for our sins,” so the death is explained, not just reported [S1]. Second, “he was buried,” which underlines that the death was real [S1]. Third, “he was raised on the third day” [S1]. Twice Paul adds “according to the Scriptures,” presenting both the death and the resurrection as fulfilling Israel’s scriptures, though the verses do not name which passages he had in mind.

Paul’s wording also matters. He “delivered” what he had “received” [S1]. The commentary notes that many scholars regard verses 3-5 as an early summary of Christian teaching that Paul had received and passed on, precisely because he introduces it with this language of receiving and delivering tradition [S2]. If so, these lines take us back to some of the earliest shared statements of Christian belief, which Paul places “first of all” in importance.
